doc.title: Leslie Gourse interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 9, 1996

title: Dignity of veteran Black musicians and racism
summary: Rowe notes their lack of bitterness; Gourse says they used humor, avoided the South and still carry prejudice from the past.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I’ve been struck by the dignity that many of these veteran African-American musicians carry with them, and when you hear about — in fact they’re not that forthcoming with some of the stories about traveling in the south and so forth, but when you do hear some of them they weathered it so well. It seems like they don’t have a lot of negative, they refuse to be negative or carry that with them — I think — for the most part.

Well I think it’s just part of not letting life in general, the negative take over. Sometimes to keep themselves sane they made up funny stories that happened to them. Sometimes they would tell stories that were very, very touching and from just one incident you get the feeling of the whole mess. And some people just wouldn’t even go south after a while, they just said, “Oh, please!” They had some bad experiences in the north too. But they tend not to dwell on it, but they are definitely affected by the history. Having met them now, from the ‘60s, ‘70s can really not comprehend what it was like for them. It would once have been impossible for me to have met them and interviewed them — if indeed anyone wanted to read about them in kind of a real way. So it’s hard. You have to put yourself — and that was not all that long ago you know. And so some of these people do have a definite prejudice against the former oppressors.
